summary: Defines three RADIUS attributes to configure and report IP port ranges and mapping behavior on devices such as carrier-grade NATs and IPv4/IPv6 translators. It lets a RADIUS server tell a device which ports a host may use.

plainLanguage.summary: A building gives each tenant certain mailbox numbers. This lets a central office tell the gate which numbers belong to whom.

questions: how does radius limit cgn ports
subtitle: Three RADIUS attributes that let a server limit, report and pre-set the transport ports a shared-address device gives each user.

tldr.problem: When many users share one IPv4 address behind a Carrier-Grade NAT, the port space has to be divided fairly, but the RADIUS server that holds each subscriber's profile had no standard way to set or learn about port behavior.
tldr.mechanism: Three new extended RADIUS attributes carry a per-user port limit, a report of allocated or deallocated port ranges, and a static port forwarding map. Their sub-fields reuse IPFIX Information Element definitions.
tldr.outcome: A RADIUS server can configure and track port use on address-sharing devices such as a CGN, NAT64 or provider WLAN gateway. The attributes are standardised in the RADIUS attribute space.

today: RFC 8045 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2017. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: Sharing Addresses and Ports
sections.content:
In a broadband network, customer data usually lives on a RADIUS server (RFC 2865). After a user is authorised, the server sends configuration to the Network Access Server (NAS), often a Broadband Network Gateway (BNG). A Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) may run on the same box, doing NAT44, NAT64 or Dual-Stack Lite AFTR work.

A CGN rewrites the source port of outgoing packets. Because many users share one IPv4 address, they also share its port number space, so each user's number of simultaneous mappings is likely to be limited by a port quota. The goal is to let the RADIUS server configure that behavior and let the NAS report back what the CGN did.

The same attributes can report an assigned port range in other settings, such as a Provider WLAN where Customer Premises Equipment manages a visiting host. The RFC focuses on IPv4 address sharing; IPv6 prefix sharing such as NPTv6 is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of families share one street address, so each family gets a set of apartment numbers. Someone has to decide how many numbers each family may use, and write down who got which.

sections.title: Terms Used
sections.content:
The RFC defines a small vocabulary. An IP port is a transport port such as a TCP or UDP port number. The IP port type is the transport protocol, given by its IP protocol number. A port range is a set of contiguous ports from a lowest to a highest number, inclusive.

The internal address and port are what a host uses behind the address-sharing device, which may be a CGN, a CPE or a Provider WLAN gateway. The external address and port are what the outside sees after translation. A mapping ties an internal address, port and protocol to an external address, port and protocol. The external address is assumed to be IPv4, while the internal one may be IPv4 or IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the building, each person has a room number. Outside, they use the building's address plus a mailbox number. A mapping is the note saying which room goes with which mailbox.

sections.title: The Three Attributes
sections.content:
All three attributes are of type tlv and are allocated from the RADIUS Extended Type space (RFC 6929). Each uses attribute Type 241 plus an Extended-Type, and holds a set of sub-attributes called TLVs.

  • IP-Port-Limit-Info (241.5) caps the number of ports a user may have, optionally for one protocol and one external IPv4 address. It MUST contain the IP-Port-Limit TLV. If no type TLV is present the limit applies to all protocols, and if no address TLV is present it applies to all IPv4 addresses of the device. The limit excludes ports that an AAA server instructs.
  • IP-Port-Range (241.6) reports a range of ports that were allocated or deallocated. It MUST contain the IP-Port-Alloc TLV, and for allocation it MUST contain both start and end TLVs. For deallocation the start and end MAY be left out, which means all previously allocated ports are freed. One port is reported by giving the same value for start and end.
  • IP-Port-Forwarding-Map (241.7) maps an internal address and port to an external port, and to an external IPv4 address if present. It MUST contain both the internal and external port TLVs, plus an internal IPv4 or IPv6 address matching the internal realm.

Permitted packets differ. The limit and the forwarding map MAY appear in Access-Accept, Access-Request (as a preference that the server need not honor), CoA-Request and Accounting-Request. The range attribute MAY appear only in an Accounting-Request.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of notes. One says how many mailbox numbers you may use. One reports which numbers were handed out or returned. One says that mail for outside box 5000 goes to room 1234.

sections.title: The Shared TLVs
sections.content:
The three attributes draw on a common set of eleven TLVs, numbered 1 to 11, with the same name and number inside each parent. Most carry an IPFIX Information Element: the limit is sourceTransportPortsLimit (458, newly defined here), the external address is postNATSourceIPv4Address (225), the internal ones are sourceIPv4Address (8), sourceIPv6Address (27) and sourceTransportPort (7), the external port is postNAPTSourceTransportPort (227), the range ends are portRangeStart (361) and portRangeEnd (362), and allocation uses natEvent (230).

IP-Port-Type holds an IP protocol number, right justified, with unused bits set to zero. Protocols with no port number, such as RSVP or ESP, MUST NOT be used. Integer values follow the 32-bit recommendation of RFC 6158, so those TLVs are six octets long. In IP-Port-Alloc, 1 means allocation and 2 means deallocation, with 0 reserved.

The last TLV, IP-Port-Local-Id, is a variable-length string. Some CGNs cannot tell hosts apart by internal IP address alone, for example when different subscribers reuse private address space, so this TLV carries an extra identifier such as a MAC address, VLAN ID or PPP session ID.
sections.plainLanguage: The three notes are built from the same small set of blanks, such as which kind of mail, which number, and which address. Each note uses only the blanks it needs.

sections.title: How It Is Used
sections.content:
When a user signs in, the NAS sends an Access-Request and the RADIUS server replies with an Access-Accept that may carry IP-Port-Limit-Info and IP-Port-Forwarding-Map. The CGN then enforces them. The limit can be changed later with a RADIUS Change of Authorization (CoA) message (RFC 5176), and the new value replaces the old once the CoA is acknowledged. The same works for the forwarding map.

A CGN may allocate blocks of ports for a user rather than one at a time. The total across all ranges MUST NOT exceed the user's limit. The CGN reports each block, with its shared IPv4 address, in an Accounting-Request using IP-Port-Range, and reports freed ranges the same way.

The RFC walks through an example. An ISP gives a user named Joe a limit of 500 ports and a forwarding map from external port 5000 to internal port 1234. The CGN allocates ports 3500 to 3540 on address 192.0.2.15, later adds 8500 to 8800, and Joe upgrades to 1000 ports through a CoA-Request.

The static map is described as complementary to the Port Control Protocol (RFC 6887): PCP lets an application on the host control its own mappings, while this document covers deployments where the AAA server instructs the mappings.
sections.plainLanguage: The front gate asks the office when you move in, and the office replies with your limit. As the gate hands out mailbox numbers, it sends a short report to the office. If you pay for more, the office sends a new limit.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document adds no new security issues beyond those already known for RADIUS (RFC 2865) and CoA (RFC 5176). If RADIUS packets travel in the clear, an attacker on the path could set a very low port limit to block a legitimate user, use many mapping entries to exhaust a user's port quota, tamper with forwarding maps so incoming traffic goes astray, or learn the address and port range assigned to a user. The root cause is the RADIUS client-to-server communication.

The IP-Port-Local-Id TLV may carry privacy-sensitive data, so identifiers without such concerns are RECOMMENDED. If an Accounting-Request contains an error, such as a bad port range, the server MUST NOT send a response (RFC 2866). The RFC targets deployments with a trusted client and server relationship, with communication optionally secured by IPsec or TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: If the notes travel in an open envelope, a sneaky person could change the numbers or peek at who has what. So the office and the gate should trust each other and use a sealed envelope.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered one new IPFIX Information Element, sourceTransportPortsLimit, with Element ID 458, data type unsigned16 and a value range from 1 to 65535. Its description ties it to the fairness requirement REQ-4 of RFC 6888.

It also assigned the three attributes 241.5, 241.6 and 241.7 from the Short Extended Space of RFC 6929, and created a registry called RADIUS IP Port Configuration and Reporting TLVs. In that registry 0 is reserved, 1 to 11 are the TLVs defined here and 12 to 255 are unassigned. New entries need Standards Action.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of numbers was updated so that everyone uses the same numbers for these notes.
